intended_object: The canonical bijection from Clifford's theory. Let V be an irreducible finite-dimensional representation of G over a field k, N a normal subgroup and W an irreducible N-constituent of Res_N V. The isotypic components of Res_N V correspond to the left cosets G/I_G(W) of the inertia group of W, with the component of g·W sent to gI_G(W). Inferred from the docstring, the module doc (Curtis–Reiner §49) and the companion simp lemmas.
explanation:
This is a canonical bijection that appears in the literature, so it counts as a mathematical object rather than an implementation device. It is built in three steps:
1. `componentsEquivOrbit` matches the isotypic components of the k[N]-module Res_N V with the G-orbit of the isomorphism class [W] in `Skeleton (FDRep k N)`. G acts there by conjugation, g•A = A∘conj(g⁻¹).
2. Mathlib's `MulAction.orbitEquivQuotientStabilizer` turns that orbit into G modulo the stabilizer of [W].
3. `Subgroup.quotientEquivOfEq` replaces the stabilizer by `inertia`, which is defined as exactly that stabilizer.

The proved lemma `isotypicComponentsEquivQuotientInertia_conjSubrepIsotypicComponent` shows that the component of the translate g·W goes to the coset gI. This is the textbook map, and it is consistent: g·W is isomorphic to the conjugate representation ^gW, and inertia is {g : ^gW ≅ W}.

Generality: k is any field, G is any group (not required to be finite), N is any normal subgroup, and V is finite-dimensional. Finite dimension is what guarantees that Res_N V is semisimple with finitely many components. It is also needed because the library takes isomorphism classes in `FDRep`, which is also why V must live in the same universe as k; that is a technical constraint, not a mathematical narrowing. The hypotheses ρ irreducible and σ an atom (a simple constituent) are exactly those of Clifford's theorem.

Mathlib has no Clifford theory, so there is no counterpart. The definition is the intended object at its natural generality.
